claim: Conscious access to sensory input can be impaired in two distinct ways: sensory input may lack sufficient bottom-up strength, or top-down attention may be directed elsewhere.
source: Conscious access to sensory input can be impaired in two distinct ways (Dehaene et al., 2006; Lamme, 2010; Mashour et al., 2020; Northoff and Lamme, 2020). Sensory input may lack sufficient bottom-up strength, or top-down attention may be directed elsewhere.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established theoretical frameworks in consciousness research.

claim: Despite both perceptual and attentional impairments resulting in a failure to perceive a stimulus, their underlying neural mechanisms are thought to be remarkably different.
source: Despite both cases resulting in a failure to perceive a stimulus, their underlying neural mechanisms are thought to be remarkably different.
evidence: Based on theoretical frameworks cited in the introduction and supported by the study's empirical findings.

claim: Influential theories of consciousness propose four stages of neural information processing associated with distinct levels of bottom-up signal strength and top-down attention.
source: Influential theories of consciousness such as global neuronal workspace and recurrent processing theory propose four stages of neural information processing associated with distinct levels of bottom-up signal strength and top-down attention.
evidence: Directly stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1A showing the four-stage model.

claim: All stimuli elicit feedforward information transfer from lower- to higher-level brain regions.
source: According to these theoretical models, all stimuli elicit feedforward information transfer from lower- to higher-level brain regions (Figure 1A, bottom row)
evidence: Stated as part of the theoretical framework and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Recurrent interactions are initiated only for stimuli with sufficient bottom-up strength.
source: but recurrent interactions are initiated only for stimuli with sufficient bottom-up strength (Figure 1A, top row).
evidence: Part of the theoretical model described and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: When stimuli are sufficiently strong and top-down attention is available, neural processing crosses a threshold, triggering global ignition that facilitates widespread recurrent interactions between frontal, parietal, and sensory cortices, yielding conscious access.
source: If stimuli are sufficiently strong and top-down attention is available, neural processing crosses a threshold, triggering a process termed global ignition, facilitating widespread recurrent interactions between frontal, parietal, and sensory cortices, yielding conscious access (Figure 1A, top left).
evidence: Describes the theoretical model with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: When top-down attention is lacking, frontoparietal network ignition is prevented, while local recurrent interactions within sensory brain regions remain relatively intact (attentional blindness).
source: Crucially, when top-down attention is lacking, frontoparietal network ignition is prevented, while local recurrent interactions within sensory brain regions remain relatively intact ('attentional blindness,' Figure 1A, top right) (Dehaene et al., 2003; Marti et al., 2015; Sergent et al., 2005; Zivony and Lamy, 2022).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Weak stimuli result in the absence, or a substantial reduction, of local recurrent interactions (perceptual blindness).
source: Weak stimuli result in the absence, or a substantial reduction, of local recurrent interactions ('perceptual blindness,' Figure 1A, bottom left) (Fahrenfort et al., 2007; Joglekar et al., 2018; van Gaal et al., 2008; van Vugt et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The four stages of the consciousness model and their underlying neural mechanisms have rarely been investigated simultaneously within the same study.
source: Although this framework is at the heart of influential theories of consciousness, the four stages of the model and their underlying neural mechanisms have rarely been investigated simultaneously within the same study (for an exception, see Fahrenfort et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement about the state of the field with one exception cited.

claim: Perceptual manipulations tend to impair overall task performance more than attentional manipulations.
source: One challenge with comparing results across different studies, or even within a study, is that perceptual manipulations tend to impair overall task performance more than attentional manipulations
evidence: Based on established patterns in consciousness research literature.

claim: Perceptual manipulations can be used to induce chance-level performance, while attentional manipulations cannot drive behavioral performance down to chance even when fully optimized.
source: Given the right parameter settings, perceptual manipulations can be used to induce chance-level performance, while it is not possible to use attentional manipulations to drive behavioral performance down to chance, even when they are optimized fully.
evidence: Based on methodological characteristics of these manipulation types.

claim: Attentional manipulations are often combined with post-hoc selection of a subset of 'blind' trials or subjects based on subjective awareness reports, which is a methodologically questionable practice.
source: For this reason, attentional manipulations are often combined with post-hoc selection of a subset of 'blind' trials (e.g. attentional blink [AB]) or subjects (e.g. inattentional blindness) based on subjective awareness reports, a methodologically questionable practice that is susceptible to criterion confounds and introduces sampling bias that leads to underestimation of consciousness (Fahrenfort et al., 2024; Peters and Lau, 2016; Schmidt, 2015; Shanks, 2017).
evidence: Methodological critique supported by multiple citations.

claim: Fahrenfort et al., 2017 found that illusory surfaces could be decoded from EEG data during the attentional blink but not during masking.
source: For example, Fahrenfort et al., 2017 found that illusory surfaces could be decoded from electroencephalogram (EEG) data during the AB but not during masking.
evidence: Direct citation of a specific finding from a previous study.

claim: In Fahrenfort et al., 2017, masking had a much stronger behavioral effect than the attentional blink, effectively reducing task performance to chance level.
source: However, masking had a much stronger behavioral effect than the AB, effectively reducing task performance to chance level.
evidence: Description of the behavioral results from the cited study.

claim: The Kanizsa illusion is supported by both lateral and feedback connections.
source: Human neuroimaging and direct neural recordings in animals have shown that the Kanizsa illusion is supported by both lateral and feedback connections (Halgren et al., 2003; Kok et al., 2016; Kok and de Lange, 2014; Lee and Nguyen, 2001; Pak et al., 2020; Wokke et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to neuroimaging and neurophysiology studies.

claim: The processing of collinear line elements primarily relies on lateral connections.
source: while the processing of collinear line elements (as in the non-illusory triangle) primarily relies on lateral connections (Bosking et al., 1997; Gilbert and Wiesel, 1979; Li, 1998; Liang et al., 2017; Schmidt et al., 1997; Stettler et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to neurophysiology studies.

claim: Differences in local contrast are processed early in the visual system through feedforward connections and are resistant to masking.
source: Differences in local contrast are processed early in the visual system through feedforward connections and are resistant to masking (Fahrenfort et al., 2007; Fahrenfort et al., 2017; Kandel et al., 2000; Lamme and Roelfsema, 2000).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Masking and the attentional blink were successfully matched for perceptual performance in the current study.
source: Importantly, paired t-tests showed that we successfully matched the key conditions, the masked condition (masked, long lag) and the AB condition (unmasked, short lag) for perceptual performance (t29=0.62, p=0.537, BF01=4.30, Figure 1D, left)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Masking and the attentional blink were successfully matched for metacognitive sensitivity in the current study.
source: as well as for metacognitive sensitivity (t29=0.72, p=0.477, BF01=4.05; Figure 1D, right, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for signal detection theory related measures of performance).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Both masking and the short T1-T2 lag impaired perceptual performance.
source: A repeated-measures (rm) ANOVA with the factors masking (present/absent) and T1-T2 lag (short/long) revealed, as expected, that both masking and the short T1-T2 lag impaired perceptual performance (F1,29=344.24, p<10–15, BF10=2.76 × 1013 and F1,29=427.54, p<10–15, BF10=3.67 × 1013)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Both masking and the short T1-T2 lag impaired metacognitive sensitivity.
source: as well as metacognitive sensitivity (F1,29=50.78, p<10–7, BF10=1.18 × 105, and F1,29=47.83, p<10–6, BF10=3.28 × 104).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Local contrast decoding peaked in a 75–95ms time window.
source: Classification performance (AUC) over time was obtained, with peak decoding accuracy in a 75–95ms time window (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, top).
evidence: Based on EEG decoding analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The peak in local contrast decoding accuracy was occipital in nature.
source: The peak in decoding accuracy was occipital in nature (see the covariance/class separability map of Figure 2A; Haufe et al., 2014), consistent with previous findings (Fahrenfort et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on topographic analysis shown in Figure 2A and consistent with previous research.

claim: Masking had a weak but statistically significant effect on local contrast decoding.
source: An rm ANOVA with the factors masking (present/absent) and T1-T2 lag (short/long) revealed a weak but statistically significant effect of masking on local contrast decoding, with the Bayes factor indicating only 'anecdotal' evidence (F1,29=6.51, p=0.016, BF10=1.31)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of EEG decoding data.

claim: T1-T2 lag had no significant effect on local contrast decoding.
source: while the T1-T2 lag had no significant effect (F1,29=0.32, p=0.578, BF01=3.45).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of EEG decoding data.

claim: There was no evidence for a difference in local contrast decoding between the performance matched masked and AB conditions.
source: A paired t-test yielded no evidence for a difference between the performance matched conditions (masked vs. AB; t29=1.42, p=0.166, BF01=2.08; Figure 2C, 'Local contrast: 75–95 ms').
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The results are in line with theoretical proposals and empirical findings that suggest limited effects of masking and attentional manipulations on perceptual processes that rely on feedforward connections.
source: These results are in line with theoretical proposals and empirical findings that suggest limited effects of masking and attentional manipulations on perceptual processes that rely on feedforward connections (Dehaene et al., 2006; Fahrenfort et al., 2007; Fahrenfort et al., 2017; Lamme, 2010)
evidence: Interpretation of results in the context of existing theory and evidence.

claim: Illusory triangle decoding revealed two prominent peaks in decoding accuracy.
source: The average of all four conditions revealed two prominent peaks in decoding accuracy, consistent with previous research (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, top) (Fahrenfort et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on EEG decoding analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and consistent with previous research.

claim: The analyses focused on two time windows: 200 to 250 ms and 375 to 475 ms after target stimulus onset.
source: Based on this previous study, our analyses focused on the averages of the two-time windows that encompassed these two peaks: specifically, from 200 to 250 ms and from 375 to 475 ms after target stimulus onset.
evidence: Methodological decision based on previous research.

claim: During the 200–250 ms time window, classification of the illusory triangle mainly relied on occipital electrodes.
source: The covariance/class separability maps (Figure 2B) indicated that during the earlier time window (200–250 ms) classification mainly relied on occipital electrodes.
evidence: Based on topographic analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The neural event at 200–250 ms likely reflects early sensory processes and may represent a marker for local recurrent processing.
source: Considering its timing, topology, and previous findings, this neural event likely reflects early sensory processes and may thus represent a marker for local recurrent processing (Fahrenfort et al., 2017; Kok et al., 2016; Roelfsema, 2006; Wokke et al., 2013; Wyatte et al., 2014).
evidence: Interpretation based on timing, topology, and previous research.

claim: The timing and topology of the later neural event (375–475 ms) overlapped with the event-related potential component P300.
source: The timing and topology of the later neural event (375–475 ms) overlapped with the event-related potential component P300 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Based on comparison with ERP data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The P300 component is associated with conscious access.
source: which is associated with conscious access (Fahrenfort et al., 2017; Sergent et al., 2005; Weaver et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The later neural event (375–475 ms) may represent a marker for global recurrent processing.
source: and may thus represent a marker for global recurrent processing.
evidence: Inference based on association with P300 and conscious access.

claim: The first illusion decoding peak (200–250 ms) was significantly impaired by both masking and T1-T2 lag.
source: Importantly, we observed a distinct difference between the performance matched conditions in the first decoding peak, which was significantly impaired by both masking (F1,29=162.62, p<10–12, BF10=5.86 × 1010) and T1-T2 lag (F1,29=78.07, p<10–8, BF10=6.03 × 106)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of EEG decoding data.

claim: The first illusion decoding peak (200–250 ms) was more affected by masking than by T1-T2 lag.
source: but importantly, it was more affected by masking than by T1-T2 lag (interaction, F1,29=18.67, p<0.001, BF10=149.92) (Figure 2C, 'Illusory triangle: 200–250 ms').
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing an interaction effect and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The first illusion decoding peak was more strongly impaired by masking than by the attentional blink in the performance matched conditions.
source: Directly comparing the performance matched conditions, the first decoding peak was more strongly impaired by masking than by the AB (t29=4.66, p<10–4, BF10=3.81).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of the matched conditions.

claim: The finding that the attentional blink allowed for greater residual local recurrent processing than masking replicates the key finding by Fahrenfort et al., 2017.
source: This suggests that the AB allowed for greater residual local recurrent processing than masking, replicating the key finding by Fahrenfort et al., 2017.
evidence: Interpretation of results in relation to previous research.

claim: The present result demonstrates that the greater local recurrency during the attentional blink reflects the difference between the perceptual vs. attentional manipulation rather than differences in behavior.
source: Importantly, the present result demonstrates that this effect reflects the difference between the perceptual vs. attentional manipulation rather than differences in behavior, as the masked condition and the AB condition were matched for perceptual performance and metacognition.
evidence: Interpretation based on the matched behavioral performance between conditions.

claim: The second illusion decoding peak (375–475 ms) was impaired by both masking and T1-T2 lag.
source: The second decoding peak was impaired by both masking (F1,29=49.75, p<10–7, BF10=8.60 × 104) and T1-T2 lag (F1,29=78.48, p<10–9, BF10=4.32 × 105)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of EEG decoding data.

claim: The matched conditions (masked and AB) did not differ significantly from each other in the second illusion decoding peak (375–475 ms).
source: and the matched conditions (masked and AB condition) did not differ significantly from each other (t29=0.21, p=0.837, BF01=5.04) (Figure 2C, 'Illusory triangle: 375–475 ms').
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There was a larger difference between the AB and the masked condition in the first than in the second illusion decoding peak.
source: Furthermore, another rm ANOVA comparing the first and second decoding peak between the matched conditions (masked/AB) revealed a significant interaction, reflecting a larger difference between the AB and the masked condition in the first than in the second decoding peak (F1,29=31.53, p<10–5, BF10=1693.17).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis comparing the two time windows.

claim: The pattern of behavioral results closely resembled the second illusion decoding peak.
source: The pattern of behavioral results, both for perceptual performance and metacognitive sensitivity, closely resembled the second decoding peak: sensitivity in all three metrics dropped from the no-manipulations condition to the masked and AB conditions, while sensitivity did not differ significantly between these performance-matched conditions (Figure 2C).
evidence: Comparison of behavioral and neural data patterns shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The similarity between late Kanizsa decoding and behavioral Kanizsa detection replicates the findings of Fahrenfort et al., 2017.
source: This similarity between behavior and EEG decoding replicates the findings of Fahrenfort et al., 2017 who also found a striking similarity between late Kanizsa decoding (at 406 ms) and behavioral Kanizsa detection.
evidence: Comparison with previous research findings.

claim: Global recurrent processing at later points in time (375–475 ms) reflected conscious access to the Kanizsa illusion.
source: These results indicate that global recurrent processing at these later points in time reflected conscious access to the Kanizsa illusion.
evidence: Interpretation based on the similarity between late decoding and behavioral measures of conscious access.

claim: Both masking and the attentional blink had stronger effects on the first illusion decoding peak compared to local contrast decoding.
source: Additional rm ANOVAs comparing the effect of the consciousness manipulations on local contrast decoding with their effects on the first and second illusion decoding peak showed that, compared to contrast decoding, both manipulations had stronger effects on the first illusion decoding peak (masking: F1,29=99.35, p<10–10, BF10=1.73 × 108; AB: F1,29=38.95, p<10–6, BF10=1.43 × 104)
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison between decoding measures.

claim: Both masking and the attentional blink had stronger effects on the second illusion decoding peak compared to local contrast decoding.
source: and on the second illusion decoding peak (masking: F1,29=22.25, p<10–4, BF10=477.25; AB: F1,29=49.60, p<10–7, BF10=3.59 × 104).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison between decoding measures.

claim: Early local contrast decoding was not improved by rendering contrast task-relevant.
source: In the light of evidence showing that unconscious processing is susceptible to conscious top-down influences (Kentridge et al., 2004; Kiefer and Brendel, 2006; Naccache et al., 2002), we ran control analyses showing that early local contrast decoding was not improved by rendering contrast task-relevant (see Appendix 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by control analyses presented in Appendix 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Masking and the attentional blink specifically influenced local and global recurrent processing, while early feedforward processing was less affected.
source: This suggests that masking and the AB specifically influenced local and global recurrent processing, respectively, while early feedforward processing was less affected.
evidence: Interpretation based on the differential effects on different decoding measures.

claim: All key findings were replicated when training the classifiers on an independent training set where individual stimuli were presented in isolation.
source: While the findings presented so far used the T1 data to train the classifiers, we replicated all key findings when training the classifiers on an independent training set where individual stimuli were presented in isolation (Figure 3A, results in Appendix 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Replication analysis using different training data, results shown in Appendix 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Non-illusory triangle decoding peaked at approximately 164 ms.
source: We trained two classifiers, one on the T1 in the RSVP task and one on the independent training set (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and tested their performance in decoding the non-illusory triangle in the T2 data, where this non-illusory triangle was always task-irrelevant. The results of both classifiers converged, and these analyses revealed a peak in decoding accuracy at ~164 ms (yielding a collinearity-only time window between 140–190 ms)
evidence: Based on EEG decoding analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The 140–190 ms collinearity-only time window was evident when classifiers were used to categorize the presence vs. absence of the Kanizsa illusion.
source: This 140–190 ms collinearity-only time window was also evident when classifiers were used to categorize the presence vs. absence of the Kanizsa illusion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, first time window), as well as in previous research (Fahrenfort et al., 2017)
evidence: Based on EEG decoding analysis and consistent with previous research.

claim: Collinearity processing contributes to Kanizsa decoding.
source: suggesting that collinearity processing also contributes to Kanizsa decoding.
evidence: Inference based on the presence of the collinearity time window in Kanizsa decoding.

claim: Both masking and the short T1-T2 lag impaired decoding accuracy in the 140–190 ms time window.
source: An rm ANOVA with the factors masking (present/absent), T1-T2 lag (short/long), and training set (illusory/non-illusory triangle) revealed that both masking and the short T1-T2 lag impaired decoding accuracy (masking: F1,29=58.95, p<10–7, BF10=8.22 × 105; T1-T2 lag: F1,29=24.90, p<10-4, BF10=776.00).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of EEG decoding data.

claim: Decoding accuracy in the 140–190 ms window was more impaired in the masked than AB condition when training was done on the illusory triangle.
source: Furthermore, paired t-tests comparing the matched conditions (masked vs. AB condition) confirmed that decoding accuracy was more impaired in the masked than AB condition, both when training was done on the illusory (t29=2.26, p=0.031, BF01=0.58)
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of matched conditions.

claim: Decoding accuracy in the 140–190 ms window was more impaired in the masked than AB condition when training was done on the non-illusory triangle.
source: and non-illusory triangle (t29=2.78, p=0.009, BF01=0.21; Figure 3C, '140–190 ms').
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There was no evidence for illusion-specific processing in the 140–190 ms window.
source: Focusing on the performance matched conditions and the role of the training set, an rm ANOVA with the factors condition (masked/AB) and training set (illusory/non-illusory triangle) on T2 illusory triangle decoding revealed no significant effect of training set (F1,29=0.09, p=0.766, BF01=4.22), i.e., no evidence for illusion-specific processing, and no significant interaction (F1,29=0.04, p=0.837, BF01=3.74).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing no effect of training set.

claim: Neural processing in the 140–190 ms window reflected collinearity-only rather than illusion-specific processing.
source: This demonstrates that neural processing in the 140–190 ms window indeed reflected collinearity-only rather than illusion-specific processing.
evidence: Interpretation based on the lack of difference between training sets.

claim: The marker for illusion-specific processing emerged in the 200–250 ms time window.
source: The marker for illusion-specific processing emerged later, namely in the 200–250 ms time window that encompassed the first illusion decoding peak reported above.
evidence: Based on the timing of when illusion-specific effects were observed.

claim: When no consciousness manipulations were applied, there was significant illusion-specific processing in the 200–250 ms window.
source: As can be seen in Figure 3B, when no consciousness manipulations were applied (unmasked, long T1-T2 lag), there was significant illusion-specific processing, i.e., T2 illusory triangle decoding was better after training a classifier on the Kanizsa illusion (collinearity-plus-illusion, green line) than after training a classifier on the non-illusory triangle (collinearity-only, purple line) (t29=4.22, p<0.001, BF10=128.47).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the 200–250 ms window, there was a significant interaction between condition (masked/AB) and training set (illusory/non-illusory triangle).
source: Turning to the performance matched conditions, an rm ANOVA with the factors condition (masked/AB) and training set (illusory/non-illusory triangle) on T2 illusory triangle decoding yielded a significant effect of condition (F1,29=16.59, p<0.001, BF10=90.73), with overall better decoding for the AB than for the masked condition, and importantly, a significant interaction (F1,29=4.65, p=0.039, BF10=2.19).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing an interaction effect.

claim: In the 200–250 ms window, decoding after training on illusory triangles was better than after training on non-illusory triangles for the attentional blink condition.
source: Figure 3B shows that decoding after training on illusory triangles (collinearity-plus-illusion) was better than after training on non-illusory triangles (collinearity-only) for the AB (t2p9=2.51, p=0.018, BF10=2.78, Figure 3B, top right)
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the 200–250 ms window, there was no difference in decoding between training on illusory vs. non-illusory triangles for the masked condition.
source: but not for the masked condition (t29=−0.02, p=0.982, BF01=5.14, Figure 3B, bottom left).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Illusion-specific processing was evident in the AB condition but fully abolished in the masked condition.
source: Thus, while illusion-specific processing was evident in the AB condition, it was fully abolished in the masked condition.
evidence: Interpretation based on the differential effects of training set between conditions.

claim: Illusion-specific processing was not affected by the attentional blink.
source: Illusion-specific processing was not even affected by the AB, as an rm ANOVA with the factors condition (no manipulations/AB) and training set (illusory/non-illusory triangle) revealed no significant interaction (F1,29=1.33, p=0.259, BF01=2.30).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing no interaction between AB and training set.

claim: The classifier trained on non-illusory triangles (collinearity-only) performed better during the AB than during the masked condition in the 200–250 ms window.
source: The classifier trained on non-illusory triangles (collinearity-only) also performed better during the AB than during the masked condition (t29=2.85, p=0.008, BF10=5.43 Figure 3C, '200–250 ms,' purple line)
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Both collinearity-only and illusion-specific processing were most strongly impaired by masking.
source: hence both collinearity-only and illusion-specific processing were most strongly impaired by masking.
evidence: Interpretation based on the pattern of results across training sets.

claim: Cross-feature decoding can isolate illusion-specific processes and does not reflect other task- or attention-related processes.
source: Control analyses presented in Appendix 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3 demonstrate that cross-feature decoding can indeed isolate illusion-specific processes and does not reflect other, e.g., task- or attention-related, processes
evidence: Supported by control analyses in Appendix 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: In the late 375–475 ms window, classifier performance was impaired by both masking and T1-T2 lag.
source: Replicating our main analysis, classifier performance was impaired by both masking (F1,29=6.01, p=0.020, BF10=2.37) and T1-T2 lag (F1,29=10.10, p=0.004, BF10=10.12)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of EEG decoding data.

claim: In the late 375–475 ms window, there were no significant differences between the two performance matched conditions.
source: with no significant differences between the two performance matched conditions (t29=−0.63, p=0.531, BF01=4.27) (Figure 3C, '375–475 ms').
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Perceptual and attentional manipulations, despite similarly impairing conscious access, exhibit distinct neural profiles in the brain.
source: We demonstrate that perceptual and attentional manipulations, despite similarly impairing conscious access, exhibit distinct neural profiles in the brain.
evidence: Summary of the main finding based on the experimental results.

claim: Early (200–250 ms, occipital) decoding of the illusory Kanizsa triangle was markedly more impaired in the masked than in the AB condition.
source: While decoding of local contrast was barely affected by the two consciousness manipulations, early (200–250 ms, occipital) decoding of the illusory Kanizsa triangle was markedly more impaired in the masked than in the AB condition (Fahrenfort et al., 2017), even though behavior was matched.
evidence: Summary of key finding with citation to previous work.

claim: Later (375–475 ms, centroparietal) illusion decoding was similarly impaired by masking and by the AB, closely resembling their matched effects on behavior.
source: By contrast, later (375–475 ms, centroparietal) illusion decoding was similarly impaired by masking and by the AB, closely resembling their matched effects on behavior.
evidence: Summary of key finding based on experimental results.

claim: Both collinearity-only and illusion-specific processing were more strongly impaired by masking than by the AB.
source: Furthermore, we differentiated between collinearity-only and illusion-specific processing and found that both processes were more strongly impaired by masking than by the AB.
evidence: Summary of key finding based on experimental results.

claim: Illusion-specific processing was unaffected by the AB, but completely abolished by masking.
source: Notably, illusion-specific processing was unaffected by the AB, but completely abolished by masking.
evidence: Summary of key finding based on experimental results.

claim: The early decoding peak for local contrast decoding (75–95 ms after target stimulus onset) likely reflects feedforward processing.
source: Based on neurophysiology and previous neuroimaging studies, the early decoding peak for local contrast decoding (75–95 ms after target stimulus onset) likely reflects feedforward processing (Fahrenfort et al., 2007; Fahrenfort et al., 2017; Kandel et al., 2000; Lamme and Roelfsema, 2000).
evidence: Interpretation based on timing and previous research.

claim: The first illusion decoding peak (200–250 ms) may be regarded as a marker of local recurrent processing.
source: The first illusion decoding peak (200–250 ms) may be regarded as a marker of local recurrent processing
evidence: Interpretation based on timing, topology, and previous research.

claim: The second illusion decoding peak (375–475 ms) likely reflects global recurrent processing.
source: while the second illusion decoding peak (375–475 ms) likely reflects global recurrent processing (Fahrenfort et al., 2017).
evidence: Interpretation based on timing, association with P300, and previous research.

claim: Both perceptual and attentional impairments leave feedforward processing largely intact and similarly impair global recurrent processing, while local recurrent processing is markedly more impaired by perceptual than by attentional impairments.
source: Thus, our findings suggest that both perceptual and attentional impairments leave feedforward processing largely intact and similarly impair global recurrent processing, while local recurrent processing is markedly more impaired by perceptual than by attentional impairments.
evidence: Summary interpretation of the overall pattern of results.

claim: This pattern of results is consistent with a previous study that used EEG to decode Kanizsa-like illusory surfaces during masking and the AB.
source: This pattern of results is consistent with a previous study that used EEG to decode Kanizsa-like illusory surfaces during masking and the AB (Fahrenfort et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison with previous research.

claim: The present study's considerably larger sample size and greater statistical power likely contributed to detecting effects where Fahrenfort et al., 2017 failed to obtain statistical significance.
source: However, the present study also revealed some effects where Fahrenfort et al., 2017 failed to obtain statistical significance, likely reflecting the present study's considerably larger sample size and greater statistical power.
evidence: Inference about methodological differences between studies.

claim: The marker for local recurrency was significantly impaired not only by masking but also by the AB, although to a lesser extent.
source: For example, in the present study the marker for feedforward processing was weakly but significantly impaired by masking, and the marker for local recurrency was significantly impaired not only by masking but also by the AB, although to a lesser extent.
evidence: Summary of findings that differ from previous work.

claim: Having matched the key conditions behaviorally, the present finding of greater local recurrency during the AB can now unequivocally be attributed to the attentional vs. perceptual manipulation of consciousness.
source: Crucially, having matched the key conditions behaviorally, the present finding of greater local recurrency during the AB can now unequivocally be attributed to the attentional vs. perceptual manipulation of consciousness.
evidence: Interpretation emphasizing the importance of matched behavioral performance.

claim: Based on neurophysiological evidence, collinearity processing primarily relies on lateral connections.
source: Although the present EEG decoding measures cannot provide direct evidence for feedback vs. lateral processes, based on neurophysiological evidence that collinearity processing primarily relies on lateral connections (Bosking et al., 1997; Gilbert and Wiesel, 1979; Li, 1998; Liang et al., 2017; Schmidt et al., 1997; Stettler et al., 2002)
evidence: Interpretation based on cited neurophysiological evidence.

claim: Processing of the Kanizsa illusion involves both lateral and feedback connections.
source: while processing of the Kanizsa illusion involves both lateral and feedback connections (Halgren et al., 2003; Kok et al., 2016; Kok and de Lange, 2014; Lee and Nguyen, 2001; Pak et al., 2020; Wokke et al., 2013)
evidence: Interpretation based on cited neurophysiological evidence.

claim: The comparison of collinearity-only to illusion-specific processing may provide insight into the components of local recurrent processing: lateral and feedback connections.
source: the comparison of collinearity-only to illusion-specific processing may provide insight into the components of local recurrent processing: lateral and feedback connections (Lamme et al., 1998; Roelfsema, 2006).
evidence: Interpretation of the methodological approach with supporting citations.

claim: Not all neurophysiological evidence unequivocally links processing of collinearity and of the Kanizsa illusion to lateral and feedback processing, respectively.
source: It should be noted that not all neurophysiological evidence unequivocally links processing of collinearity and of the Kanizsa illusion to lateral and feedback processing, respectively (Angelucci et al., 2002; Bair et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2014)
evidence: Acknowledgment of complexity in the literature with citations.

claim: Overlap in decoding the illusory and non-illusory triangle may reflect feedback processes representing the triangular shapes.
source: so that overlap in decoding the illusory and non-illusory triangle may reflect other mechanisms, for example, feedback processes representing the triangular shapes as well.
evidence: Alternative interpretation acknowledging complexity.

claim: The decoding results suggest that lateral processing occurred earlier (140–190 ms after target stimulus onset) than illusion-specific feedback processing (200–250 ms).
source: However, following our reasoning, the decoding results suggest that lateral processing occurred earlier (140–190 ms after target stimulus onset) than illusion-specific feedback processing (200–250 ms), in line with animal research (Angelucci and Bressloff, 2006; Lamme et al., 1998; Roelfsema, 2006).
evidence: Interpretation of temporal sequence based on data and consistent with animal research.

claim: Both lateral and feedback processing were more strongly affected by masking than by the AB.
source: Both lateral and feedback processing were more strongly affected by masking than by the AB
evidence: Summary of findings regarding the two types of processing.

claim: The 'attentional blindness' stage of the four-stage model of consciousness involves both lateral and feedback connections.
source: indicating that the 'attentional blindness' stage of the four-stage model of consciousness (Figure 1A) involves both lateral and feedback connections.
evidence: Interpretation relating findings to the theoretical model in Figure 1A.

claim: Masking had a stronger effect on illusion-specific feedback processing than on lateral processing.
source: Furthermore, masking had a stronger effect on illusion-specific feedback processing than on lateral processing.
evidence: Comparison of effects on different types of processing.

claim: Current theories do not distinguish between the roles of lateral vs. feedback connections for consciousness.
source: As current theories do not distinguish between the roles of lateral vs. feedback connections for consciousness
evidence: Statement about the current state of theoretical frameworks.

claim: The present findings may enrich empirical and theoretical work on perceptual vs. attentional mechanisms of consciousness.
source: the present findings may enrich empirical and theoretical work on perceptual vs. attentional mechanisms of consciousness (Block, 2005; Dehaene et al., 2006; Hatamimajoumerd et al., 2022; Lamme, 2010; Pitts et al., 2018; Sergent and Dehaene, 2004)
evidence: Statement about the potential impact of the findings with citations to relevant theoretical work.

claim: The findings clearly distinguish the neural profiles of each processing stage of the influential four-stage model of conscious experience.
source: clearly distinguishing the neural profiles of each processing stage of the influential four-stage model of conscious experience (Figure 1A).
evidence: Summary of the contribution to understanding the four-stage model.

claim: The findings suggest a processing sequence from feedforward processing to local recurrent interactions encompassing lateral-to-feedback connections, ultimately leading to global recurrency and conscious report.
source: Along with the distinct temporal and spatial EEG decoding patterns associated with lateral and feedback processing, our findings suggest a processing sequence from feedforward processing to local recurrent interactions encompassing lateral-to-feedback connections, ultimately leading to global recurrency and conscious report.
evidence: Synthesis of findings into a proposed processing sequence.

claim: Compared to masking, the AB left local recurrent processing intact, while feedforward processing did not differ between the two manipulations.
source: Our results suggest that, compared to masking, the AB left local recurrent processing intact, while feedforward processing did not differ between the two manipulations.
evidence: Summary of key findings comparing the two manipulations.

claim: Local recurrent processing plays a critical role in perceptual integration, facilitating the organization of fragmented sensory information into a coherent whole.
source: Local recurrent processing plays a critical role in perceptual integration, facilitating the organization of fragmented sensory information, such as lines, surfaces, and objects, into a coherent whole (Roelfsema, 2023).
evidence: Statement about the functional role of local recurrent processing with citation.

claim: The EEG decoding results support the notion that local recurrent processing plays a critical role in perceptual integration.
source: Our EEG decoding results support this notion, demonstrating that the AB allows for greater processing of collinearity and the illusion specifically within a time window spanning 140–250 ms after stimulus onset, likely reflecting sparing of local recurrent processes in visual cortex (Fahrenfort et al., 2017; Kok et al., 2016).
evidence: Interpretation of results in relation to the functional role of local recurrent processing.

claim: The findings align with established models of the AB phenomenon, in which the AB reflects a late post-perceptual central bottleneck characterized by limited attentional capacity.
source: This aligns with established models of the AB phenomenon, in which the AB reflects a late post-perceptual central bottleneck characterized by limited attentional capacity (Shapiro et al., 1997)
evidence: Interpretation relating findings to existing models of the AB with citation.

claim: Sensory information presented during the AB can undergo extensive processing, allowing for perceptual integration, possibly even leading up to semantic analysis.
source: so that sensory information presented during the AB can nevertheless undergo extensive processing, allowing for perceptual integration, possibly even leading up to semantic analysis (Luck et al., 1996).
evidence: Statement about the extent of processing during AB with citation.

claim: The findings do not imply that unconscious high-level processing can only occur during inattention.
source: Clearly, these findings do not imply that unconscious high-level (e.g. semantic) processing can only occur during inattention, nor do they necessarily generalize to other forms of inattention.
evidence: Clarification of the scope and limitations of the findings.

claim: While the AB represents a prime example of late attentional filtering, other ways of inducing inattention or distraction may filter information earlier in the processing hierarchy.
source: Indeed, while the AB represents a prime example of late attentional filtering, other ways of inducing inattention or distraction (e.g. by manipulating spatial attention) may filter information earlier in the processing hierarchy (e.g. Luck and Hillyard, 1994 vs. Vogel et al., 1998).
evidence: Discussion of how different types of attentional manipulations may have different effects, with citations.

claim: Preserved local recurrent processing during the AB is consistent with classic load theory.
source: Preserved local recurrent processing during the AB is also consistent with classic load theory (Lavie and Dalton, 2014)
evidence: Interpretation relating findings to load theory with citation.

claim: According to load theory, increasing perceptual load more strongly reduces distractor processing than increasing cognitive load.
source: where increasing perceptual load (Lavie and De Fockert, 2003) more strongly reduces distractor processing than increasing cognitive load (e.g. by engaging working memory, as in our AB condition).
evidence: Statement about load theory with citations.

claim: According to load theory, perceptual and attentional manipulations serve as early and late filters for incoming sensory information, respectively, resulting in more extensive processing under inattention.
source: According to this theory, perceptual and attentional manipulations serve as early and late filters for incoming sensory information, respectively, resulting in more extensive processing under inattention.
evidence: Statement about the implications of load theory.

claim: One neuroimaging study found that only perceptual but not cognitive (working memory) load decreased fMRI activity in the parahippocampal place area in response to distractor scenes.
source: Indeed, one of the few neuroimaging studies that included both manipulations found that only perceptual but not cognitive (working memory) load decreased fMRI activity in the parahippocampal place area in response to distractor scenes (Yi et al., 2004)
evidence: Citation of a specific neuroimaging finding.

claim: Not all neuroimaging evidence is consistent with a stronger effect of perceptual than cognitive load.
source: although not all neuroimaging evidence is consistent with a stronger effect of perceptual than cognitive load (Brockhoff et al., 2022).
evidence: Acknowledgment of inconsistent findings in the literature with citation.

claim: The impact of inattention vs. masking can depend on the neural architecture required for the task at hand.
source: Furthermore, previous research has shown that the impact of inattention vs. masking can depend on the neural architecture required for the task at hand.
evidence: Statement about task-dependent effects with reference to previous research.

claim: Processes related to the detection of conflicting response tendencies are more susceptible to inattention than to masking.
source: For example, processes related to the detection of conflicting response tendencies, a hallmark of cognitive control and strongly associated with the prefrontal cortex (Ridderinkhof et al., 2004), are more susceptible to inattention, which reduces the depth of stimulus processing (Nuiten et al., 2021) than to masking, restricting recurrent interactions, but allowing for deep feedforward processing (all the way up to prefrontal cortex) (Jiang et al., 2018; van Gaal et al., 2008).
evidence: Example of task-dependent effects with multiple citations.

claim: Deep feedforward processing can be sufficient for unconscious high-level processing, as indicated by a rich literature demonstrating high-level processing during masking.
source: Such deep feedforward processing can be sufficient for unconscious high-level processing, as indicated by a rich literature demonstrating high-level (e.g. semantic) processing during masking (Kouider and Dehaene, 2007; Van den Bussche et al., 2009; van Gaal and Lamme, 2012).
evidence: Statement about unconscious processing during masking with citations.

claim: Rather than enabling deep unconscious processing, preserved local recurrency during inattention may afford other processing advantages linked to its proposed role in perceptual integration.
source: Thus, rather than enabling deep unconscious processing, preserved local recurrency during inattention may afford other processing advantages linked to its proposed role in perceptual integration (Lamme, 2020), such as integration of stimulus elements over space or time.
evidence: Interpretation of the functional significance of preserved local recurrency with citation.

claim: Thirty participants took part in the final experimental session.
source: The remaining 30 participants (22±3-y-old, 10 men, two left-handed) took part in the final (main experimental) session.
evidence: Statement of sample size for the main experiment.

claim: The study was approved by the local ethics committee.
source: The study was approved by the local ethics committee.
evidence: Statement about ethical approval.

claim: Participants gave informed consent.
source: Participants gave informed consent and received research credits or 15 euros per hour.
evidence: Statement about informed consent.

claim: The target stimulus set had a 2×2×2 design, resulting in eight stimuli.
source: The target stimulus set had a 2 (illusory Kanizsa triangle: present/absent)×2 (non-illusory triangle: present/absent)×2 (rotation: present/absent) design, resulting in eight stimuli (Figure 1B).
evidence: Description of the stimulus design shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Three aligned Pac-Man elements induced the Kanizsa illusion.
source: Three aligned Pac-Man elements induced the Kanizsa illusion.
evidence: Description of the stimulus feature.

claim: The non-illusory triangle was present when the stimuli's three other elements (the 'two-legged white circles') were aligned.
source: The non-illusory triangle was present when the stimuli's three other elements (the 'two-legged white circles') were aligned.
evidence: Description of the stimulus feature.

claim: Differences in local contrast were created by rotating the entire stimulus by 180 degrees.
source: Differences in local contrast were created by rotating the entire stimulus by 180 degrees.
evidence: Description of the stimulus manipulation.

claim: The shortest distance between the edges of the three Pac-Man stimuli as well as between the edges of the three aligned two-legged white circles was 2.8 degrees of visual angle.
source: The shortest distance between the edges of the three Pac-Man stimuli as well as between the edges of the three aligned two-legged white circles was 2.8 degrees of visual angle.
evidence: Specification of stimulus parameters.

claim: Neuronal responses to collinearity in primary visual cortex are most robust when the distance between elements is smaller than 2.8 degrees.
source: Although neuronal responses to collinearity in primary visual cortex are most robust when this distance is smaller (Kapadia et al., 1995; Kapadia et al., 2000)
evidence: Statement about neurophysiological properties with citations.

claim: Longer-range lateral connections between neurons with similar orientation selectivity can span distances corresponding to visual angles considerably greater than 2.8 degrees.
source: longer-range lateral connections between neurons with similar orientation selectivity can span distances corresponding to visual angles considerably greater than 2.8 degrees (Bosking et al., 1997; Stettler et al., 2002).
evidence: Statement about neurophysiological properties with citations.

claim: The experiment consisted of three separate sessions conducted on different days: a 3 hr session to collect EEG data for the independent training set, a 1.5 hr practice session, and a 3 hr experimental session.
source: The experiment consisted of three separate sessions conducted on different days: a 3 hr session to collect EEG data for the independent training set, a 1.5 hr practice session, and a 3 hr experimental session.
evidence: Description of the experimental procedure.

claim: T1 was presented for 67 ms to improve the decoding analyses' training dataset.
source: To improve the decoding analyses' training dataset, T1 was presented for 67 ms.
evidence: Methodological decision with rationale.

claim: The longer presentation duration of T1 facilitated attending to T1, which should result in greater deployment of attentional resources and thereby increase the size of the AB.
source: The longer presentation duration facilitated attending to T1, which should result in greater deployment of attentional resources and thereby increase the size of the AB.
evidence: Rationale for methodological decision.

claim: Mask contrast was adjusted using a staircasing procedure to match performance in the AB condition.
source: Importantly, mask contrast in the masked condition was adjusted using a staircasing procedure to match performance in the AB condition, ensuring comparable perceptual performance in the masked and the AB condition across participants (see Methods for more details).
evidence: Description of the method used to match performance.

claim: EEG was recorded at 1024 Hz using a 64-channel ActiveTwo system.
source: EEG was recorded at 1024 Hz using a 64-channel ActiveTwo system (BioSemi).
evidence: Description of EEG recording parameters.

claim: The data were downsampled to 128 Hz.
source: Finally, the data were downsampled to 128 Hz.
evidence: Description of data preprocessing step.

claim: Linear discriminant classifiers were trained on the T1 data and tested on the T2 data.
source: For each participant and each visual feature, a linear discriminant classifier was trained on the T1 data and tested on each condition of the T2 data.
evidence: Description of the decoding analysis method.

claim: AUC was used as the performance measure for decoding.
source: AUC was again used as the performance measure.
evidence: Description of the performance metric.

claim: Cluster-based permutation testing was used to correct for multiple comparisons.
source: We used cluster-based permutation testing (1000 iterations at a threshold of 0.05) to correct for multiple comparisons (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007).
evidence: Description of the statistical method with citation.
